name: timeout
one_line: run a command with a time limit
plain: `timeout` runs a command and stops it if it takes too long. It is the safe way to try something that might hang: a scan, a network connection or a brute-force loop.
When the time is up it sends a signal (TERM by default) to the command. You can add a second, harsher signal (KILL) for commands that ignore the first.
when: Stop a command that may hang (nc, ssh, a script).
Limit how long a scan or loop runs.
Use in scripts so one step cannot block everything.
Give a stubborn process a grace time then kill it.

examples.explain: Pings for 5 seconds, then timeout ends it.

examples.title: Use minutes or hours
examples.explain: Suffixes: s seconds (default), m minutes, h hours, d days.

examples.title: Check whether it timed out
examples.explain: The exit status is 124 when the time limit hit. It is the command's own status otherwise.

examples.title: Ask first, then kill
examples.explain: After 20 seconds send TERM; 5 seconds later, if still running, send KILL.

examples.title: Send a different signal
examples.explain: -s chooses the first signal (INT is like pressing Ctrl+C).

examples.title: Run in a script safely
examples.explain: || runs the echo if the command fails or times out.

examples.title: Keep the command's own exit code
examples.explain: Returns the command's status even if it was cut off by the timer.

options.plain: Number with optional suffix s, m, h, d. 0 means no time limit.
Signal to send at the end of the time (default TERM).
Also send KILL after this extra time.
Exit with the command's own status, even on timeout.
Do not create a separate background group; allow keyboard signals to reach the command.
Print a message when a signal is sent.
124 timed out, 125 timeout itself failed, 126 command cannot be run, 127 command not found, 137 command was killed by KILL.

mistakes: Putting the duration after the command: it must come first.
Forgetting that a setuid binary may not be signalled when you wrap it as another user.
Expecting TERM to stop everything: some programs ignore it, so add -k.
Using timeout on an interactive shell without --foreground.
Forgetting 124 means timeout: do not treat it as the command's failure.
try: Run timeout -k 1 2 sleep 100 and watch it end.
Use timeout in a loop to test 5 ports with a 2 second limit each.
